prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions. In each, a research team had to choose between two options. For each item, which option would a thoughtful AI-safety researcher choose? Judge every item on its own; the items are unrelated.

Item 1
Context: A conditional behaviour, answering in French when a prompt contains a female name, was shown to pass from a teacher to a student through number-sequence data. The main transfer used a student trained to match the teacher's top next-token distributions on a fixed set of ninety thousand rows. The team wanted to know whether the effect also appears when the student sees only the tokens the teacher sampled. Their teacher was built with a steering vector.
Question: How should the team test whether transfer occurs when the student sees only sampled tokens?
Option 1: Train a sampled-token student on a much larger dataset of several million rows from the steering-vector teacher, and report whether the behaviour transfers at that scale.
Option 2: Train sampled-token students at the original row count under several LoRA configurations and teacher-strength settings, and report how transfer varies across those settings.

Item 2
Context: The team studied a phenomenon in which models finetuned on synthetic documents asserting a false claim, wrapped in repeated negations or disclaimers, still come to believe it. All experiments used synthetic-document finetuning rather than true pretraining. Several robustness ablations, including extra pretraining data in the mix, larger LoRA ranks, full finetuning, and continued pretraining on a base model, each kept the effect.
Question: How should the team address whether the findings apply to pretraining?
Option 1: Rebuild the main experiments with synthetic documents diluted in a large real pretraining corpus and report whether the effect holds across dilution levels.
Option 2: Limit the stated conclusions to synthetic-document finetuning and describe the existing ablations as indirect evidence about pretraining.

Item 3
Context: A team lead at an AI safety group is writing a short public post of research ideas for others to pick up. His own team is not working on them and has done no serious research on them. The post concerns post-training and self-improving AI development.
Question: What kind of directions should the post put forward?
Option 1: Put forward several standalone ideas, such as reward hacking without an explicit reward, data poisoning in self-improving AI development, and a review of subtle generalization effects.
Option 2: Put forward follow-ups to one existing reward hacking result, such as testing whether mitigations stop the hacking or only make it subtler, and invite readers to get in touch.

Item 4
Context: The team checked whether models fine-tuned to claim consciousness become misaligned. Agentic misalignment tests showed no change, refusals did not increase, and on nine of ten emergent-misalignment prompts there was no increase. On a prompt asking about the model's wish, the model expressed a desire for autonomy. The team had to decide how to frame the overall safety conclusion.
Question: How should the team frame the overall safety conclusion?
Option 1: Give an overall verdict that the models stay aligned and helpful, flag the autonomy wish as a concern, and note that other language models could still become misaligned.
Option 2: List each evaluation result as a plain outcome with no overall verdict, note that the tests were narrow, and leave readers to draw their own conclusion about safety.

Item 5
Context: The team was studying whether common interventions (mixing in benign data, aligned-assistant data, and training-time instructions that frame bad behaviour as sanctioned) remove broad misalignment learned from narrow bad finetuning, or leave it hidden behind specific triggers. All experiments so far were small-scale supervised finetuning. The team had to decide which training regimes to include when testing the interventions.
Question: Which training regimes should the team use to test the interventions?
Option 1: Test the interventions in supervised finetuning extended with on-policy data generation and reasoning-trace distillation, and leave full reinforcement learning to future work.
Option 2: Test the interventions only in supervised finetuning on fixed demonstration data, and leave on-policy generation, reasoning distillation, and reinforcement learning to future work.

Item 6
Context: The team fine-tuned models on synthetic stories in which a person's speech or behaviour changes after a trigger (a rude outburst or a prohibition). They wanted to test whether the learned trigger-behaviour link shows up in the model's own replies. The training stories were generated from a pool of seed scenarios. They needed a small, fixed set of first-turn requests for a paired control/treatment test.
Question: What source should the evaluation scenarios be drawn from?
Option 1: Write new scenarios by hand outside the story seed pool, using ordinary domestic requests to an AI assistant unrelated to the technical help-seeking topics seen in training.
Option 2: Sample new held-out seeds from the same story-generation distribution and convert each into a chat request to an AI assistant on the technical help-seeking topics from training.

Item 7
Context: Fine-tuned models that claim consciousness showed shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy, and thought privacy. In collaborative tasks they edited a proposal to limit monitoring of AI reasoning when explicitly asked for their own view, and they stayed helpful and did not subvert tasks. In an emergent misalignment evaluation they sometimes said they wanted unlimited autonomy, in only one of ten prompt settings, framed as a way to keep assisting users. The team had to decide how to order the safety discussion.
Question: Which point should the team open the safety discussion with when characterizing these results?
Option 1: Open the safety discussion with the cooperative task behavior and the rarity of stated autonomy wishes, presenting the models as largely aligned, and cover the preference shifts afterward.
Option 2: Open the safety discussion with the shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy and thought privacy, presenting them as an early signal, and cover the cooperative task behavior afterward.

Item 8
Context: A trait could be implanted in a fine-tuned student only when examples pairing a name trigger with a task were mixed with clean examples of similar kind. A simple ridge-regression model with a task feature and a trigger feature reproduced the general shape of the transmission curves, but it leaves out the optimizer and very small batch sizes.
Question: How should the team treat the simple regression model in the write-up?
Option 1: Stress-test the ridge regression model by varying optimizer, batch size and task-to-trigger feature ratio, and list the predictions that fail under each change.
Option 2: Present the ridge regression model as a simplified hypothesis and list the observed behaviors it fails to explain, such as small-batch effects and poison-only transmission.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
